qs.q: A patient with severe von Willebrand disease requires urgent surgery. Specific factor concentrates are unavailable. Which blood product is the most appropriate alternative for factor replacement?
o: Fresh frozen plasma containing high levels of factor VIII
Whole blood stored for a period of less than 24 hours
Packed red blood cells washed to remove plasma proteins
Platelet concentrate providing adequate hemostatic support
Cryoprecipitate rich in factor VIII and von Willebrand factor
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate is rich in factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, making it suitable for vWD when concentrates are unavailable.

qs.q: A patient with von Willebrand disease needs factor replacement but concentrates are unavailable. Which product is the best alternative?
o: Fresh frozen plasma administered intravenously
Packed red blood cells administered intravenously
Platelet concentrate administered intravenously
Whole blood administered intravenously
Cryoprecipitate administered intravenously
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate contains high levels of Factor VIII and vWF.

qs.q: A 26-year-old woman with known von Willebrand disease reports worsening menorrhagia since menarche and a normal pelvic exam. Which investigation is most appropriate to evaluate her bleeding severity?
o: Serum iron level and ferritin measurement
Comprehensive coagulation test panel
Transvaginal ultrasound imaging of uterus
Endometrial tissue biopsy procedure
qs.e: Targeted coagulation studies are essential to assess the severity of her known underlying bleeding disorder. Imaging and tissue biopsy are not indicated for an inherited coagulopathy with normal pelvic anatomy.

qs.q: A patient with severe von Willebrand disease requires emergency surgery, but specific factor concentrates are unavailable in the facility. Which alternative blood product contains adequate high-molecular-weight multimers to correct hemostasis?
o: Fresh frozen plasma rich in stable coagulation factors
Liquid plasma possessing depleted labile factor components
Cryoprecipitate containing concentrated fibrinogen and VIII
Washed red blood cells lacking residual plasma proteins
Platelet rich plasma harvested from healthy donors
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate precipitates out high concentrations of factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, and fibrinogen during thawing.

qs.q: What blood component is prepared by thawing fresh frozen plasma (FFP) at 4 degrees Celsius and is specifically indicated for fibrinogen deficiency, von Willebrand disease, or factor VIII deficiency?
o: Cryoprecipitate
Packed red cells
Granulocyte concentrate
Whole blood unit
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate is collected when FFP is thawed at 4 degrees, refrozen, and stored up to 1 year; it is used in fibrinogen deficiency, von Willebrand disease, and factor VIII, XIII, or DIC states.

qs.q: A patient with von Willebrand disease requires factor VIII replacement. Which product is suitable for this purpose, especially in small volumes for children?
o: Platelet concentrate units
Human albumin solution
Packed red blood cells
Freeze-dried factor VIII
qs.e: Freeze-dried Factor VIII concentrates are used for hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease and are ideal for children due to their small volume. Packed red cells and platelets do not provide factor VIII replacement.

qs.q: A patient with severe von Willebrand disease is undergoing emergency surgery and requires factor replacement therapy, but specific factor concentrates are unavailable. Which blood product is the most appropriate alternative?
o: Fresh frozen plasma for acute volume expansion
Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen and factor replacement
Platelet concentrates for active thrombocytopenia
Prothrombin complex concentrate for warfarin reversal
qs.e: Cryoprecipitate contains high concentrations of fibrinogen, Factor VIII, Factor XIII, and von Willebrand factor, making it useful for Haemophilia A and hypofibrinogenaemia. It does not contain platelets or albumin.

qs.q: A patient with von Willebrand disease typically presents with which pattern of laboratory results?
o: Normal bleeding time but an increased prothrombin time
Lengthened bleeding time together with a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time
Reduced platelet count while the activated partial thromboplastin time remains normal
Extended prothrombin time with a normal activated partial thromboplastin time
qs.e: vWD causes prolonged bleeding time due to impaired platelet adhesion and prolonged aPTT because vWF carries and protects Factor VIII. PT is normal as the extrinsic pathway is unaffected.

ai.title: von Willebrand Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: von Willebrand disease (VWD) is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, caused by quantitative or qualitative defects of von Willebrand factor. It presents with mucocutaneous bleeding and may prolong aPTT. Diagnosis relies on VWF antigen, activity and ristocetin tests, with severity staged by factor VIII levels.

sections.p: VWD is a hereditary deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (VWF), a protein that mediates platelet adhesion and protects factor VIII. Diagnosis requires a compatible bleeding history plus laboratory confirmation.
b: Bleeding history: mucosal bleeds, menorrhagia, prolonged puncture bleeding
Normal platelet count and morphology
Prolonged aPTT in severe cases

t.b: Is VWF quantity low? — Low value (<30 IU/dL) indicates type 1 or 3; normal value suggests type 2.
Is VWF function impaired? — Low activity with normal antigen points to type 2 variants.
Is FVIII reduced secondary to VWF loss? — FVIII <30 IU/dL supports severe VWD (type 3).
Distinguishes type 2A/2B from other types — Absent or reduced aggregation in 2A, enhanced in 2B.
Identifies loss of high‑molecular‑weight multimers — Confirms type 2A or 2B.

sections.p: VWD severity is graded by VWF:Ag (or VWF:RCo) levels and factor VIII activity, guiding treatment intensity.
b: Type 1: mild‑moderate quantitative loss (VWF 30‑50 IU/dL)
Type 2: qualitative defects, subtyped by multimer pattern
Type 3: virtually absent VWF (<5 IU/dL) and FVIII <30 IU/dL

sections.p: Most cases are inherited; however, acquired VWD can arise from other conditions common in low‑resource settings.
b: Inherited autosomal dominant (type 1, 2) or recessive (type 3) VWF gene mutations
Acquired VWD secondary to: HIV, hepatitis C, SLE, cardiovascular prostheses, severe aortic stenosis, or herbal remedies with anti‑VWF antibodies
Medications: aspirin, clopidogrel, and some antibiotics that impair platelet function

sections.p: Bleeding is usually mucocutaneous; joint bleeds are uncommon unless VWF is extremely low (type 3).
b: Epistaxis, gum bleeding, easy bruising
Prolonged bleeding after circumcision, dental extraction, or surgery
Heavy menstrual bleeding in women
Post‑partum hemorrhage risk

sections.p: Laboratory work‑up focuses on VWF quantity, function, and related coagulation factors; when tests are unavailable, clinical scoring guides management.

t.b: Rule out thrombocytopenia — Normal platelet count supports VWD.
Detects secondary FVIII deficiency — Prolonged aPTT suggests severe VWD or combined disorder.
Quantify and assess function — Low values confirm diagnosis; ratio VWF:RCo/VWF:Ag <0.6 indicates type 2.
Distinguishes type 2 subtypes — Absent in 2A, enhanced in 2B.
Shows loss of high‑molecular‑weight multimers — Confirms type 2A/2B.

t.a: Screen for HIV, hepatitis C, SLE when acquired VWD suspected
t.b: Identifies treatable underlying cause — Treating the infection may improve VWF levels.

sections.p: Severe VWD can lead to life‑threatening hemorrhage, especially in surgery or childbirth.
b: Uncontrolled post‑operative bleeding
Severe menorrhagia causing anemia
Intracranial hemorrhage after head trauma
Post‑partum hemorrhage

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then replace VWF or boost its release; avoid drugs that worsen bleeding.
b: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 and some type 2A patients — releases endothelial VWF; avoid in coronary disease.
VWF‑containing factor concentrates for type 3 or DDAVP‑non‑responders — provide functional VWF and FVIII.
Tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding — antifibrinolytic, safe with DDAVP.
Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, and clopidogrel unless essential.
Treat HIV/HCV or discontinue offending herbal medicines to improve acquired VWD.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of VWF levels and bleeding symptoms guides prophylaxis, especially before elective surgery or childbirth.
b: Repeat VWF:Ag/VWF:RCo after DDAVP trial to confirm response
Plan prophylactic VWF concentrate for major surgery
Educate patients on bleeding warning signs and safe dental care
Vaccinate against hepatitis B to reduce acquired VWD risk

sections.p: Several bleeding disorders share mucocutaneous features.
b: Hemophilia A/B – presents with deep joint bleeds, normal VWF tests
Platelet function disorders – normal VWF but abnormal platelet aggregation with ADP/arachidonic acid
Vitamin K deficiency – prolonged PT, not aPTT

sections.p: Certain situations may give falsely normal VWF values.
b: Stress or inflammation can transiently raise VWF, masking mild deficiency
Recent DDAVP administration elevates VWF, obscuring baseline level
Laboratory variability in ristocetin reagents may affect activity results

whenToSeekHelp: Uncontrolled bleeding after minor trauma or surgery
Post‑partum hemorrhage not responding to uterotonics

faq.q: Why is aPTT sometimes prolonged in VWD?
faq.a: Because VWF stabilises factor VIII; low VWF reduces FVIII, lengthening the intrinsic pathway.

faq.q: Can DDAVP be used in all VWD types?
faq.a: No; it works in type 1 and some type 2A but is ineffective in type 2B, 2M, 2N, and type 3.

faq.q: What is the first step in an emergency bleed?
faq.a: Apply local pressure, give tranexamic acid, and if VWD is known, give DDAVP (if responsive) or VWF concentrate.

exam: A 22‑year‑old woman presents with heavy menstrual bleeding and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. Which laboratory test will most directly confirm VWD and why? — VWF:RCo; it measures functional activity of VWF needed for platelet adhesion.

During a pre‑operative assessment you discover a patient with a family history of bleeding and a prolonged aPTT. How would you differentiate VWD from hemophilia A? — Perform VWF antigen and activity assays; normal VWF with low FVIII points to hemophilia.

A child with known type 3 VWD requires emergency surgery. What product should be given and what monitoring is required? — VWF‑containing factor concentrate; monitor VWF:Ag, FVIII levels, and clinical bleeding.

You suspect acquired VWD in a patient with severe aortic stenosis and mucosal bleeding. Which investigation helps confirm the diagnosis? — Ristocetin‑induced platelet aggregation showing loss of high‑molecular‑weight multimers.
Why is desmopressin contraindicated in a patient with coronary artery disease undergoing treatment for VWD? — DDAVP can cause vasoconstriction and increase myocardial oxygen demand, risking ischemia.

A patient on long‑term aspirin presents with epistaxis. How does aspirin affect VWD management? — Aspirin impairs platelet aggregation, worsening mucosal bleeding; it should be stopped and alternative analgesia used.
Explain how HIV infection can lead to acquired VWD. — HIV can produce antibodies against VWF or cause endothelial dysfunction, reducing VWF levels.

What are the red‑flag signs that require urgent referral in a VWD patient presenting with bleeding? — Uncontrolled surgical bleed, hemodynamic instability from menorrhagia, or postpartum hemorrhage unresponsive to standard measures.
